name: Pravega

archived.reason: Core development slowed sharply in March 2024 after the main contributing organisation moved its team to other work. The last release, 0.13.0, dates from September 2023 and the last commit from March 2025, and the CNCF archived the project in September 2025 after a vote of its Technical Oversight Committee. Some use continues in EU research projects, but there are no maintainers for the core.

summary: A stream storage service from Dell that kept events in Apache BookKeeper and moved them to long-term storage, with streams that split and merge their segments automatically as load changes; archived by the CNCF in 2025.
intro: Pravega stores streams: durable, append-only, unbounded sequences of events, grouped into scopes. Each stream is split into segments, and each event carries a routing key that decides its segment, so events with the same key are read in the order they were written. Unlike a Kafka topic, the number of segments isn’t fixed: under a data- or event-rate scaling policy a hot segment splits in two and cold neighbours merge, and readers in a reader group are rebalanced across the new segments. Writers can batch events in transactions that become visible only on commit, and readers persist their positions, so applications such as Flink jobs can process each event exactly once. A state synchronizer lets distributed processes share state through a stream with optimistic, conditional updates.

Two kinds of server do the work. A controller, the control plane, creates, scales and deletes streams. The segment store, the data plane, writes incoming events first to Tier 1 storage, built on Apache BookKeeper, for low-latency durability, and later moves them to Tier 2 long-term storage such as HDFS, a file system or an object store, from which old data can still be read through the same stream API. The project was written in Java, licensed under Apache 2.0 and released 0.13.0, its last version, in September 2023.
strengths: Streams scale their segments up and down automatically with load, without a fixed partition count
One API covers both fresh events in BookKeeper and old data in long-term storage, so streams can be kept indefinitely
Per-key ordering, transactions and exactly-once reading built into the client
Apache 2.0 code that can still be studied as a design for elastic, tiered stream storage
limits: Archived: no releases since September 2023, no commits since March 2025, and no maintainers for the core
Never reached 1.0, and its clients (Java, plus Rust, Python, Node.js and C#) and Flink and Spark connectors are a far smaller ecosystem than Kafka’s or Pulsar’s
Running it meant a controller, a segment store, BookKeeper, ZooKeeper and a long-term store

worksWith.how: moves older data (Tier 2) to HDFS in
has connectors for exactly-once jobs in

story: Dell engineers started Pravega in 2016 to give streaming data a storage primitive like a file or an object: unbounded, durable, strictly ordered, and elastic enough to follow changing load without anyone resizing partitions. They built it on Apache BookKeeper for the hot tail of each stream and on Dell’s own Isilon and ECS storage, or HDFS, for the long tail, and released 0.1.0 under Apache 2.0 in September 2017.

Pravega joined the CNCF Sandbox in November 2020. In March 2024 work on it dropped sharply after the main contributing organisation changed priorities, and in June 2025 the CNCF heard that the original team had been disbanded. A maintainer argued that two EU research projects, NEARDATA and CLOUDSKIN, still used it, but with no core development for over a year the TOC voted to archive it, and it was archived on 23 September 2025, free to reapply if active development resumes.

choices.why: Fixed partition counts force users to guess future load; letting segments scale with event or byte rate keeps per-key order while the stream grows and shrinks.

choices.choice: Two storage tiers behind one API
choices.why: BookKeeper gives low-latency durable writes but is costly for years of data; moving segments to HDFS or object storage keeps history cheap while readers see one continuous stream.
Stream processors like Flink need reader positions and transactional writes they can checkpoint, so Pravega built both into its client API.

timeline.text: Development starts at Dell; repository created in July
Accepted into the CNCF Sandbox on 10 November
Core development drops off in March
Last commit in March; CNCF archives the project on 23 September
